content.text: Master Chen, our hospital union is currently organizing a group purchase. This time, the apples are shipped directly from the origin—they're large and sweet. I’ll send you a screenshot of the order list. If your colleagues in the fleet are interested, you can join the group order together. The more we buy, the better the discount. Alternatively, do you drivers have any similar internal benefit channels? This reminds me of our last discussion about family meal planning, where we both emphasized the quality of ingredients. This group purchase method should be perfect for busy families like yours.

Thank you, Nurse Fang. Let me take a look. This chain message is quite well-organized, just as clear as the hypoglycemia management chart you shared before, with steps that are easy to follow at a glance. The apples look good, and I happen to be running low on them at home. Our bus company sometimes distributes some labor protection supplies, such as towels and laundry detergent. They have strong stain-removing power, though the packaging is plain, which aligns well with the "practicality first" idea you mentioned earlier.

Yes, this is exactly the kind of apple I was talking about. I took a real photo for you. Look at the color and freshness—it's much better than those that have been sitting in supermarkets for too long. The laundry detergent your company provides sounds practical, just like the cleaning effectiveness we emphasized when discussing cafeteria hygiene. I remember you took photos of the grease stains in the driver's cafeteria kitchen—this kind of strong cleaning detergent would be perfect for that.

Indeed, the apple looks quite tempting. I recall when you shared your meal prep plan earlier, the neatly arranged containers in the refrigerator also emphasized the quality of ingredients. This small-scale group buying, built on trust, feels more reliable than blindly shopping on e-commerce platforms. In our driver group, we sometimes share discount information from partner gas stations, which is also a form of resource exchange—similar to the community mutual aid model we discussed when promoting the idea of a health corner.

That's right, I also joined group buys for rice and oil. Let me send you a picture. The rice grains are plump, and the oil is clear—both are daily essentials. Just like when we handle feeding stray dogs, we emphasize that a fixed source brings more peace of mind. Group buying is also based on reliable channels. If any of your drivers need anything, I can help coordinate group orders. This reminds me of the time you chose a spine-protecting backpack for your son—you also asked around for recommendations. Doing thorough research before shopping is really important.

The rice and oil look to be of good quality, and my household might need to restock as well. This group-buying method reminds me of the community mutual aid mentioned in the Healthy Corner initiative, where scattered needs are brought together. However, Nurse Fang, we must be careful to distinguish authenticity and guard against scams when participating in group purchases. I’ve heard that some group buys lure people in with low prices, but the goods don’t match the description. Just like when we discussed food safety earlier, you reminded me to avoid restaurants with obvious grease stains—shopping also requires a keen eye for detail.

You're right, Master Chen. Our union is quite well-organized, with established suppliers and a solid reputation built over time. It's similar to how you emphasized observing school entrances and researching word-of-mouth when choosing a spine-protecting backpack. If you drivers have similar channels, feel free to share them—we can all benefit from mutual cooperation. From the hypoglycemia incident to TNR education, the foundation of our collaboration is based on practical needs and reliable information.

This is the detergent our company recently distributed, and I took a photo of it. The stain removal effect is really good, and the packaging is simple. I think this kind of work-related benefit is more practical than blindly chasing advertisements, just like when we discuss food safety, we focus on actual results rather than appearances. The design of this bottle reminds me of the picture of the 84 disinfectant you posted earlier—both are practical products that prioritize functionality.

The detergent looks practical, with simple packaging but strong functionality, which reminds me of your focus on grease cleaning when you shared observations about the cafeteria. If you drivers need apples or rice oil, I can tally the quantities and place a joint order. This kind of resource exchange can save everyone time and money. Just like the meal prep plan we discussed earlier, planning ahead improves efficiency, allowing us to use the saved time for more important things.

Good idea, Nurse Fang. I'll ask my colleagues in the fleet to see how many people need apples. Additionally, our company sometimes collaborates with local farms to provide seasonal vegetables at discounted prices. If you're interested, I can share the information, just like how you shared the contact details for the stray animal rescue group during the TNR awareness session, to pass along reliable resource channels.

That's fantastic! The vegetable group purchase sounds both healthy and cost-effective, aligning perfectly with our value of prioritizing prevention. We can set up a simple information-sharing group to regularly update everyone on such benefits, helping everyone avoid being misled by false promotions on e-commerce platforms. This is like the 'Health Corner' we envisioned, but extended from a physical site to online information sharing—both are essentially about community mutual aid.

I agree. Based on our previous collaborations, such as the hypoglycemia incident and the health corner initiative, this trust relationship makes shopping more reassuring. I will promote this idea in the driver group to encourage everyone to participate and form a small consumer mutual aid network. I recall that when we dealt with feeding stray dogs last time, we also mentioned the need to develop community understanding. This time, we are extending that understanding into the realm of shopping.

Yes, this way shopping becomes more community-oriented and personal. Just like how you handled the care for the stray dogs by focusing on community collaboration and establishing fixed feeding points. We can start with a pilot program for group purchases of apples, and if it goes well, expand to other items, ensuring quality and reliability. This is similar to how we approach any community project—starting small and steadily progressing.

Okay, Nurse Fang. Based on my preliminary count, about five or six colleagues are interested in the apples. I’ll remind everyone to pay attention to the group purchase details, such as confirming the origin and freshness, to avoid receiving spoiled goods like some e-commerce deliveries. Your thoughtfulness always helps us avoid risks, just like when you compiled the guide to avoiding pitfalls when eating out and the quick visual guide for stir-fried shredded pork with green peppers—simplifying and visualizing complex issues.

Thank you for your trust, Master Chen. I will ensure the group buying process is transparent and keep everyone updated on the progress promptly. This reminds me of when we shared meal preparation plans, where we both emphasized practicality and efficiency. I hope this model can operate in the long term and benefit more community members. From in-carriage first aid to family nutrition and now collective shopping, our areas of collaboration are expanding, but the core remains 'extraordinary in the ordinary.'

I believe so. Looking back at our historical conversations, whether it's about food safety or animal welfare, we have always turned issues into scalable solutions. This group purchase and mutual assistance initiative is another example of how ordinary roles can demonstrate extraordinary value. I will continue to provide updates on the progress, just as I previously shared with you the company's evaluation of the health corner concept.

Agreed, Master Chen. Our collaboration is becoming increasingly smooth, expanding from specific events to systematic community support. I look forward to the success of the group purchase for apples, and in the future, we can share more resource information to make shopping simpler and more heartfelt. Just as we always say, safety first, life wisdom, and community mutual aid—these small efforts, when gathered together, bring about change.

Alright, it's settled then. I'll start by gathering the specific needs from my colleagues and then send them to you. Thank you for always bringing such practical suggestions, Nurse Fang. It's been over half a year since the hypoglycemia incident in February, and our discussions have expanded from health to all aspects of life, each time bringing new insights. Let's talk again soon!

You're welcome, Master Chen. I've also learned a lot of practical experience from you, such as keen observation and social adeptness. Let's stay in touch, and I'll follow up on the group purchase. As we always say at the end of our conversations, community health depends on everyone's efforts! Goodbye!
